Falconbridge by Amax. That did not come to pass, but I wonder what would happen to our industry and what kind of controls we would have if a company was solely owned from outside the country. Would it have the caring for the country and for the area in which it mines which a company that is at least partially owned in our own country would have? That worries me far more and I think we definitely have to take some very close looks at the trends of multinationals taking over some of our natural resources.
Another point that worries me very much is the monetary policy of this government, the high interest rates which lead to the high value of our dollar. I realize that it is far more difficult for our mines to make a profit when the value of our dollar is as high as it is. It is important that we maintain those profits so that the profits can be put back into our economy at a local level as well as at a national level.
I am also very worried that we will neglect the environment. That is a major issue. We in Sudbury, in Inco and Falconbridge, have done some tremendous things towards pollution abatement. As a matter of fact, I think in many ways Sudbury could be used as a model in terms of greening. I would certainly invite anyone to come to our community and see the types of investments that have been made, even through tough times, in our community on protection of the environment.
I would conclude by saying that I do support the motion. I think it is important that we pressure the provincial government, or at least exert our influence as a federal government, in ensuring that as much as possible what we produce here is refined here.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak on this issue of processing mineral resources in Canada.
Before I do so, I would like to refer back to the actual motion, wherein it says:
- the government should consider the advisability of developing programs and policies to promote further processing of all extracted materials produced by Canadian mines-
This indicates to me one of the fundamental flaws in the motion. It says all resources must be further processed. It shows, I think, the lack of understanding of the hon. member proposing the motion, particularly with regard to the coal industry, with which I have some experience. I do not know how he imagines we are going

October 10, 1989
Private Members' Business
to further process coal before we export it. Perhaps some explanation of the industry and the process is required.
When coal is exported to be used in utilities and to make electricity in foreign lands, the only thing that is done to it before it is used is that it is pulverized. Now, if we did that pulverizing here in Canada the coal would be absolutely impossible to handle. You cannot ship pulverized coal. It would plug up all of the equipment, it would be a complete mess in terms of the environment and so forth.
Certainly we cannot say that we wish to upgrade every mineral resource that is produced in Canada. That is one particular example where it would be categorically impossible, unless of course the hon. member wishes to actually make the electricity in Canada and put it in boxes and ship it out. I am sure that when that technology is available Canadian industry would be pleased to do it because one of the biggest problems we have in exporting coal is the cost of transportation. I am sure it will be many, many years before a technology of that nature is available.
The hon. member wants us to do everything possible to encourage the processing of minerals in Canada. I am very surprised that he should say that because his party is on record as opposing the goods and services tax which is, of course, directed at making our resource producers more viable and more economical. If we want to encourage processing in Canada, then we want to make our industries as viable as we possibly can. That extra income, the revenue that comes from having lower operating costs, will encourage them to upgrade resources further. This, of course, is an objective that we all share. I am pleased, as I say, to speak on this subject today.
I think it is important to understand something about the presence of downstream processing of raw materials in Canada, and the extent that this presence varies from commodity to commodity. In cases where Canada's domestic end-use market is substantial, downstream processing is often well established. Examples of this would be, of course, the aluminum and cement industries. In other cases, the pattern is predominantly determined by the presence of high tariff and non-tariff barriers in important foreign markets. These tariff barriers increase with the degree of processing and pose a major hurdle for Canadian expansion in this area.
It is in recognition of the problems posed by these trade barriers that this government completed the free trade agreement with the United States. Canada is also firmly committed to tariff reduction through the multilateral trade negotiations now under way at the GATT. We are confident that with the removal of trade barriers, as a result of the FTA and tariff reductions, we will see significant additional growth in the further processing of minerals and metals in Canada.
This future growth, indicated by market forces, will be assisted by this government's efforts aimed at enhancing Canada's reputation as a safe and attractive haven for investment, both foreign and domestic. This includes maintaining a fiscal regime which imparts no disadvantage to our producers.
Earlier I stated that Canada already has a strong presence in further processing of minerals. It is well known that over 80 per cent of Canada's mineral production is exported. It is often believed that the bulk of these exports is in the form of ores or concentrates. This is simply not true. Let me review the metal mining sector, a sector which alone accounts for over 70 per cent of Canada's mineral production.
One hundred per cent of all nickel ore produced in Canada is upgrade into nickel matte in this country. Furthermore, some two-thirds of this is refined in Canada. About 94 per cent of our gold production in 1987 was upgraded in Canada, and some 75 per cent of the silver concentrates were processed in this country as well. Over 50 per cent of copper and of zinc concentrates received upgrading in Canada. These commodities alone constitute about 60 per cent of the metal mining sector's output in any given year.
I would like to provide a little more detail about our copper industry. The Canadian copper industry is made up of two distinct groups, the west coast concentrate producers and the central eastern integrated producers. Rail transport of concentrates from British Columbia to eastern Canada for domestic processing is an expensive proposition. It is far more economical and attractive to
October 10, 1989

ship concentrates to Japan for refining than to transport them across Canada.
The possible construction of a world-scale copper smelter in British Columbia has been studied but has not been found to be a viable proposition. I am confident that companies will continue to evaluate new possibilities as conditions change, and that if such a proposition becomes viable that they will undertake it.
While this government wishes to encourage further processing of minerals and metals in Canada, it must be careful how this is accomplished. It is preferable that this should come about without direct government intervention. It is well to remember that while we are a leading exporter of minerals concentrates, we are also an important importer of ores and concentrates. For example, we rely exclusively on imported bauxite and alumina for our aluminum industry.
We also need foreign copper concentrates to supply our smelters in eastern Canada. In order to maintain production at Cominco's Trail smelter, significant supplies of zinc concentrate will have to be imported when that company's huge Red Dog deposit in Alaska comes on stream in 1990.
Some nickel concentrates are already obtained from offshore for domestic refining. Imports of these are expected to increase next year when the Sherritt Gordon refinery acquires additional raw material for its operations.
It is evident that Canada should not take measures to promote downstream processing in a way that will provide grounds for any retaliatory action by those countries on whom we depend for some of our raw materials.
Looking at the non-metal business, it is worth noting that Canada is a leading exporter of coal and potash. I would like to point out that these commodities accounted for over $2.5 billion in export earnings in 1987. There is little scope for further upgrading of these items, as I mentioned earlier, particularly in regard to coal.
Canada does not lack for recent improvements to its downstream processing facilities. Let me give you some examples. In the case of zinc, the Trail smelter has been
Private Members' Business
expanded, the Valleyfield smelter has been modernized, and Kidd Creek continues to be state-of-the-art.
While Canada does not mine the raw materials for aluminum, the aluminum industry is, nevertheless, a good example of new developments in the further processing of raw materials in this country. Thanks to the investment climate created by this present government, component manufacturers have chosen to locate here and to take advantage of the presence of this industry.
The aluminum industry continues to move aggressively into further processed forms. In 1988, Alcan announced construction of a new $3 million plant to produce ceramic-related materials for use in composite products, and a $25 million plant to manufacture dural, a ceramic particle reinforced aluminum in the Lac-Saint-Jean region of Quebec. Alcan will also build a new alumina hydrate plant at a cost of $28 million. This material is used in artificial marble, toothpaste and rubber backings for carpets.
A $112 million aluminum auto parts plant is being built in Quebec by a French company. This facility to be constructed in Riviere-Beaudette will produce precision cast aluminum parts including cylinder heads and intake manifolds for the automobile industry.
Earlier this year, Reynolds Metals announced plans for a $50 million plant plant in Louiseville, Quebec, that will produce cast aluminum wheels. This plant will employ some 325 people.
Another interesting new development is taking place in platinum. Traditionally, the platinum content of Canadian nickel matte has been recovered offshore. Now, a pilot plant to recover platinum from spent catalysts has started in Toronto. If successful, it may be adapted to handle the platinum content of domestic mineral concentrates.
Canada's steel industry is maintaining its position as a world leader and competitive producer by employing new technologies. The percentage of Canadian steel that is continuous cast far exceeds the level in the United States, and we have one of the most modem pipe and tube plants in the world. The steel industry has plans for a new galvanizing plant in Hamilton and expects to apply technologies which will move us away from the use of coke in the blast furnace. These programs will move our

October 10, 1989
Private Members' Business
supply capability further downstream and ensure a cleaner environment in industrial areas.
Canada is on the verge of becoming the world's largest producer of magnesium metal. If all planned or potential magnesium smelting projects are implemented by 1994, total capital investment in this sector could amount to more than $1 billion, creating more than 1,000 new jobs. Canada's next producer of magnesium metal, Norsk Hydro, should have its plant at Becancour, Quebec, in production shortly. This facility expects to employ approximately 350 permanent workers.
Other projects are under active consideration. For example, Noranda Minerals Inc. and Lavalin Inc. have announced their intention to proceed to the feasibility stage of their Magnola joint venture which will be based on asbestos tailings from the Thetford Mines area. Magnesium International Corporation and Alberta Natural Gas Limited are constructing a magnesium metal plant at Aylderside near High River, Alberta.
Canada's record on further processing is promising, but this government will continue to strive for improvement. Even now a considerable number of developments are under way that will improve our performance. These are examples of how this government has encouraged a well established industry to move further down the path of higher value-added activities. I am confident that this trend will continue as and when trade barriers are reduced as a result of our concerted actions with the free trade agreement and the GATT negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, I think as the member for Calgary North rightly pointed out, we should really read the resolution again so that we can make sure we discuss the points that are relevant. We have heard the comments about mineral extraction and the processing of minerals in Canada. Yet the resolution, if I might re-read it for you, states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of developing programs and policies to promote further processing of all extracted materials produced by Canadian mines in Canada, and to discourage the export of unprocessed minerals from Canada.
It is interesting that the resolution switched from "materials" to "minerals". I am not sure what happened to all those other things that might not be classified as minerals in the discussion.
In my riding we have some substantial landfill sites provided to us courtesy of the city of Toronto. We are not necessarily happy to have them, but now there have been some proposals put forward that state that there might be some extraction opportunities of the wealth of energy and resources that are buried in these particular mountains, if I might call them appropriately.
When we talk about materials extraction, do we talk about iron? Obviously we must. We must talk about coal, uranium, nickel, peatmoss, copper, potash, limestone, zinc, cement-goodness, I bet you the list could go on. I think there are some 120 different identified minerals in the world. I think we have most of them in Canada, at least a substantial portion of them. I do not know if we can just talk about a very limited aspect. Of course, what is not mentioned in all this is where in fact do we as Canadians who want to process these products sell them.
As the Member for Calgary North rightly indicated, there are some products that we extract from the earth that really require no processing when they are ready for use. Certainly, he is very knowledgeable on the coal industry and made a very valid point. I suspect that the same may apply for example when we extract from the earth such things as oil, natural gas, and even water. I am not sure if a conventional thing called mining should always be considered. Mining is regarded as digging a hole in the ground to see what is down there. I am sure that is the old philosophy. The new philosophy in mining is such that I am sure that many things we do would in one sense or another be regarded as mining.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, I am a member of the finance committee dealing with the goods and services tax and have been travelling across Canada, at least to this point in time to western Canada, and soon to embark on a swing through eastern Canada, to hear the input of constituents. We have veiy clearly as a government identified that resource sector industries, particularly in western Canada and eastern Canada, would really benefit by the goods and services tax. I think it is very appropriate that we have had some comment about the
October 10,1989

coal industry. The coal industry came forward and very solidly embraced the concept of the goods and services tax.
It even estimated that each individual mine that it represents in western Canada in particular would become more profitable on average to the tune of some $500,000 per year. Half a million dollars may not be much, but it is half a million dollars that can be invested in technology. The industry can invest it in the creation of new jobs. When it buys technology it buys equipment. The industry buys things manufactured somewhere else in Canada, hopefully, even right in its own backyard or wherever the mine happens to be.
On the other side, as I mentioned, the finance committee less than a half hour ago had a presentation from the Hon. Mr. Douglas who was the Minister of Finance in New Zealand and who made some very enlightening presentations on the goods and services tax. As you know, the governing party is considered the left wing or socialist party of New Zealand. I think it caused some considerable problem to the members of the NDP caucus who sit on the Finance Committee because everything that was being said about the GST in New Zealand went so diametrically opposite to what the NDP is saying here in Canada. Yet, this was fellow brethren of the socialist societies of the world speaking to each other taking such a diametrically opposite point of view.
The one thing that Mr. Douglas commented on was that in New Zealand the practice has been to target industries and provide government assistance to those industries to do things. Since the Labour Party of New Zealand has taken over it has done away with that. It has done away with tax grants, incentive grants or, as is mentioned in this motion, programs and policies. It has done away with all of those things to business. The party's argument is that business ought to do what business deems right.
It has also done away with a lot of other programs. This Labour government had to admit that less government interference in the targeting of industries has in fact been very beneficial to New Zealand. Here we have before us a resolution which states that we ought to interfere in business and not let it do its own thing. Yet in New Zealand a government of the same stripe as some members of this House says that this is exactly wrong and
Private Members' Business
that there ought to be less interference, with the end result that your industries will be better off.
I find that to be a very enlightening comment. Of course, it is nice to be able to say that we will process in Canada all of the things that we mine out of the ground. We will not get into specific items as to what they are at this particular point. That is great. We will process all these things. Then what will we do with them? It would be really nice to have a market in Canada where all these things could be sold. That would be just absolutely fantastic. Since there are only 25 million of us and not 250 million, we have a problem.
We have the ability in Canada to produce and to extract from the earth many more resources than we have the ability to consume ourselves. What do we do with these things? Do we just leave them in the ground until Canada's population is at 250 million? I guess we could come up with more grants to families to encourage them-not unlike as has been done in the province of Quebec-to have more children. I am not sure that that would get us to 250 million in a real hurry.
In the riding next to me, in the riding of Oshawa, the automotive industry, for example, is a very prominent employer. It is rather prominent in my riding as well. What does the automotive industry do? Ultimately, you can say that it processes extracted materials, whether it is steel, metals of one kind or another, or aluminum. It processes things and it sells them. In fairness, it sells the majority of those products produced in those plants in the riding next to me in some other country, not in Canada.
I would hazard to say that if we followed the policy of only selling those products that we extract to Canadians, then we would have a problem. It does not work. On the other hand, if we put in place rules that make that happen obviously our trading partners, wherever they are around the world, will erect barriers that will make it very difficult for us in Canada to sell things. Yes, that means in some cases, that we will have to sell products that are extracted from our rich resources and not processed. But what it does do is it provides us with a tremendous opportunity to sell processed products. Those processed products start to work to our advantage, as is very clear.

October 10,1989
Private Members' Business
We do not operate in isolation to other countries. We do not operate in isolation to various trading arrangements that exist in the world. In fact, as members of the GATT, we have substantial trading relationships. Any policies that would interfere with the free flow of goods I would find very difficult to support because the agreements we have with trading partners encourage free flow in both directions. Yes, we win on some and we lose on others. We have a number of substantial winners which I hope in a future presentation, Mr. Speaker, you will allow me to speak on. I could go on for a half hour at least talking about the winners that we have in Canada on resource extraction.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to share with the House some special feelings about the mining industry of Canada because, as the House will know, I served for two years, between 1984 and 1986, as the Minister of State for Mines. In that two-year period I enjoyed the learning process which is the privilege of all who serve in these capacities. But for me, as an engineer, it was a very special introduction to the magnificence of Canada's mining sector.
As members of the House will recall, the international cycle for commodities, particularly some of the main products of Canada, cycled very badly in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The industry had presented to government year after year the need for attention to their interest to reinforce the industry so that it could come back and compete when the cycles rejoined in the future.
As minister, I was privileged to meet with the leaders of our great mining companies in Canada and to learn of their capacities and their technologies and their very special concerns. In retrospect, I am pleased to have been able to serve as minister during a period in which those cycles did turn around. The very hopes and prospects of the industry which had been set out by the industry to the government and which the government accepted through its leaders in the Energy, Mines and Resources Department turned around.
I should not pass that reference to the department without giving credit to the men and women who have served Canada as technology leaders in the Can Labs
that Canada sponsors jointly in working with the private sector. The doctors of technology who have established and guided those centres across Canada have done a wonderful job and are part of this rebuilding process, this further processing or refining process that we are discussing today.
As my memory goes back to those occasions together, I remember from the very beginning the need for consultation and the need for working in concert with the provincial governments. Our Constitution very specifically addresses the rights to mineral wealth to the provinces. I learned, as many of our colleagues here will know, that there was a division between the federal authority and the provincial authority which often confused and frustrated the mining industry. Mines ministers' conferences were never quite complete in much the way that Canada's discussions on its Constitution are not complete because Quebec was not there.
I was privileged to preside over and chair the first mines ministers' conference in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, at which the provincial Minister of Mines for Quebec, one of the three very large provincial ministries in mines, was present and participated fully, raising the same concerns for the mining industry that we all did. We looked for harmony and harmonization of the regulations so that mining decisions to explore, to develop, to exploit, to operate, were all addressed with a fairness or a unity for Canada so that it was not one province out-bargaining the other in terms of advantage.
The primary function of the Canadian Government in this process was to reinforce the magnificence, the potential of our mining industry. I remember another incident which was that a series of conditions in our finance legislation provided for what were then known as flow-through shares. It was a mechanism or a treatment of investments which went into the development or exploration for mining potential which is a tremendous risk.
I learned that while some of us look at investments as having a return within so many years, perhaps over a period of 10 years, for many mining ventures it was 10 years before they started to operate and begin to recover the front-end risk money which had gone in 10 years earlier. This is a tremendous expression of confidence in Canada's ability and in a mine's ability to ride through a
October 10, 1989

cycle and then compete with all the others which are looking for the world markets.
I think it was my colleague from Ontario who pointed out this need to recognize that we are in a world market and that others can meet the demands of this market like anyone else.
I am going to be very disappointed this afternoon because I can see that the clock is going far too fast and I know you are not going to allow me, unless we get unanimous consent, another half hour. I will do my best to finish in the two or three minutes you are going to allow.
The uranium deposits with which Canada is blessed can continue to become for safe and peaceful purposes a tremendous resource in Canada, both in Ontario and particularly now in Saskatchewan. A special facility, Eldorado, was built at Port Hope, not far from the riding of Ontario. The competition which that processing plant found became an international concern in trade and in relationships with the U.S.
Major users of uranium in the U.S. would wish to buy the uranium in its raw form and direct it to the refining plants in the southern United States and then process it into their uranium thermal plants. This was fine except that we had a capacity which was efficient and modern. We added to that capacity in Port Hope, and further refining was done but always with the recognition that we had to compete with the access to the same materials through other means. We have tremendous competitors in this world when it comes to our mining products. The Australians are in a great position to compete with Canadians because their mines are just as rich, and their resources are just as strong.
I hope that this motion will be considered as time goes by, recognizing that the real need is for Canadians. I see you are almost on your feet, Mr. Speaker, so I will not stretch this out too long.
I want to give credit to the member from Calgary North who also raised a number of important points in his address to this House this afternoon. As I say, Mr. Speaker, I know you are going to have to watch the clock, it is your duty, and I honour you for it. Thank you very much for this occasion.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CONFERENCE BOARD OF CANADA REPORT-NATIONAL SALES TAX-IMPACT ON BUSINESS INVESTMENT
THE ECONOMY-CONFERENCE BOARD OF CANADA REPORT-NATIONAL SALES TAX-IMPACT ON BUSINESS INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words about the 9 per cent manufacturers' sales tax that the government plans to introduce on January 1, 1991.
I want to refer to an issue I raised in Question Period, regarding the report presented to the country by the Conference Board of Canada. At that time, the Conference Board vice president and chief economist, Mr. James Frank, issued a number of observations that I thought would be worth presenting to the Minister of Finance.
The Conference Board of Canada we all recognize as being the most prestigious and the most objective economic think-tank and projection firm in Canada. Their track record has been impeccable in terms of predicting the impact of various government programs, and their researchers and reports can be rated as nothing short of outstanding.
Their latest report on the goods and services tax indicates that inflation will increase, economic growth will be reduced, and that more than 70,000 jobs will be killed in the first year of the goods and services tax. To put it more precisely, the Conference Board of Canada suggests that inflation will increase to 7.3 per cent from 5 per cent, in 1991.
As a result of the hearings in various parts of Canada, we have heard that the labour movement certainly sees this as a reason to be requesting significant increases in pay packages. If inflation is going to increase by 7.3 per cent and the tax will add another 9 per cent to the cost of most goods and services, we are looking at requests

October 10, 1989
Adjournment Debate
coming in at 16 per cent in one year. Along with the indication from the manufacturing and retail sector that prices will have to be increased to reflect the increased costs associated with the sales tax, it means that prices will go up, and wages and salaries will have to go up to meet this increased cost of living.
When the cost of living goes up, or as I might also state it, the inflation rate goes up, the Governor of the Bank of Canada will feel obligated to raise interest rates accordingly. As the Minister of Finance has indicated, we can expect the interest rates to go up a number of percentage points as a result of the goods and services tax which will further strangle any hope of economic growth, particularly in the regions of Canada.
The Conference Board of Canada goes on at some length to point out some of the concerns that they have regarding this government proposal. I must say that they reflect much of what I have been hearing in communities like Clearwater, Chase, Barriere, Kamloops, Logan Lake, Westwold, Savona and many other smaller communities within my own constituency, where people really make four points. Whether they represent small business, homeowners, tourist operations, loggers, farmers, ranchers, restaurateurs, seniors, students, or whatever group, they remind us of the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada promised that if a sales tax was going to be introduced, we would be promised and guaranteed four items.
One, the tax would be visible for all to see. Well, the Prime Minister has had to renege on that promise because we now know that in many cases it will simply be built into the price of a service or a commodity and the public will never see the fact that there is a 9 per cent federal sales tax.
The Prime Minister promised that it would be revenue neutral. That is the second promise that he broke, because now the Prime Minister has indicated that it will not be revenue neutral, that this tax will raise $5.5 billion beyond what the present manufacturers' sales tax presently raises.
The Prime Minister also promised that the federal sales tax would be integrated with the provincial sales tax and we would have only one tax to pay that would be termed a sales tax. That promise has also been broken, because now we know that the federal government will
first of all impose its 9 per cent tax and then on top of that the provincial governments that have a sales tax will impose their provincial sales tax, which means they will be taxing taxes.
The Prime Minister said that it would be very simple. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which represents 80,000 small businesses across Canada, states that this is going to be a red-tape nightmare, that this system is too complex to consider introducing and too expensive to introduce.
On the matter of the goods and services tax, groups like the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the Canadian Organization for Small Business, virtually every agricultural organization in Canada and now, lastly, the Conference Board of Canada, the most prestigious board in the country with regard to predicting the economic implications of various government initiatives, are condemning the sales tax and saying that this will squeeze economic life out of our economy. They have asked the government to go back to the drawing board. They join with groups like the New Democratic Party which also have been saying: "Let's go back to the drawing board. Let's look at real tax reform of our tax system rather than have a regressive sales tax that discriminates against the regions of Canada and the poorer people of the country. Let's have real tax reform that is fair, just and equitable".

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CONFERENCE BOARD OF CANADA REPORT-NATIONAL SALES TAX-IMPACT ON BUSINESS INVESTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer my Hon. New Democratic colleague and you will allow me to begin by pointing out how sweet it is to hear the New Democratic Party finally support these arguments, along with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the small business federation, although they usually condemn the Chamber of Commerce and its members, condemn small business, etc. But this time, they support it.
On the other hand, my colleague perhaps made two small mistakes in his presentation, Mr. Speaker. In the first place, he said that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business do not support the new tax. That is false. Every
October 10, 1989

organization, Mr. Seaker, which appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance told us:
"First, the present federal sales tax is bad for Canada; the present federal sales tax must be changed. Now, in the context of your proposed GST, we would like to see some things done differently." Great! Everyone, even my colleague, the Finance critic, condemns the present federal sales tax. I listened to my constituents and I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I also go around my riding, to Pointe-du-Lac, Saint-Severe, Saint-Barnabe, Trois-Riveres-Ouest or Trois-Rivieres, and people tell me that they know the tax will be visible, because businesses will be very glad to put it on the bill, saying, "This is the federal government's tax, not profit we are making."
Second, people are aware that the tax will bring in more revenue, but they are very glad that the extra revenue will be returned to them. All families whose income is under $30,000 a year will get a tax credit.
Third, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister never insisted that the tax must be federal-provincial. He always said that he would prefer it, but we know that the provinces refused.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, small businesses, as I was told again lask week in Pointe-du-Lac, are very glad to know that they will get $600 a year to administer a tax that can fit on an 8 x 12 page.
Mr. Speaker, those are the points that I wanted to make. The tax will be simpler, fairer and more equitable for Canadians and for business.

subtopic: FISHERIES-IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA-CRISIS IN ATLANTIC INDUSTRY
FISHERIES-IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA-CRISIS IN ATLANTIC INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Burin-St. George's has 158 communities, the majority of which are very heavily involved in the fishery, and a number of which are involved in the deep sea fishery. For example, we have deep sea plants at Burgeo and Ramea, at Gaultois and Harbour Breton, at Fortune and Grand Bank, at Marys-town and at Burin.
I tell you that, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it goes a long way toward explaining why it is I have been raising, on a regular basis, the issue of the current state of the fishery.
Adjournment Debate
Indeed, the item on the agenda to which we are now speaking, the so-called late show or adjournment debate, actually arises out of a question that I put to the Minister of Fisheries on or about June 20.
For at least four months we have been talking about this issue and during that time I have been characterizing the current state as a crisis. The Minister has disagreed with me. As recently as Monday past, just eight days ago, he took exception. If we look at Hansard, we see that he chose quite different wording to characterize the current state of the fishery. He said that in most respects, fishermen in Atlantic Canada are enjoying a year which is prosperous and adequate for their needs.
Almost any fisherman, almost any plant worker in Atlantic Canada, can vouch for the fact that the minister's statement is simply not true. It is just not true. The question arises, why is the minister, aided and abetted, I may say, by the gentleman from St. John's West who I guess may be responding to these few remarks of mine, choosing to send out what is clearly a false signal? I can only guess that somebody has come up with a strategy to downplay the issue. They are not going to convince anybody who is actively involved in the fishery. They are certainly not going to convince anybody involved in the Newfoundland fishery, either the inshore or the deep-sea fishery, that there is no crisis. They are not going to convince any of those people that the fishery in Newfoundland is not on the verge of collapse.
They certainly are not going to convince the Newfoundland government from whom the Government of Canada has had in its hands this report for two months, a report rightly entitled "Resource Crisis in the Newfoundland Fishery". The report goes into some detail to spell out the dimensions of that crisis. It refers in part to the overfishing by the European community.
To give a quick example, in 1986, NAFO, the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization, assigned to the European Community countries 26,295 tonnes as its quota for that particular year; in round figures, 26,000 tonnes. In that year, countries in the European Community fished not 26,000 but 160,000 tonnes or about six times as much as the quota would allow. The figures are similar for succeeding years.

October 10, 1989
Adjournment Debate
One, there is a crisis. Two, is there any wonder that there is a crisis? Third, I say to the minister and his parliamentary secretary that if there is no crisis, what is the Minister for International Trade doing overseas? Four years after it started, he has now discovered there is overfishing. He is now going to go out there and do a selling job. Well, bully for him. You have heard about closing the gate after the horse was gone.
This is a classic case of where this government has obfuscated, tried to cover up and be wishy-washy in terms of the issue and finally, too late, talking out of both sides of its mouth, the one hand saying there is no problem, there is no crisis, and the other hand going out to try to put out some fires.
It is beyond the bushfire stage. The fishermen, the plant workers that I represent, know there is a problem and they know the very serious dimensions of the problem. If we were to pursue this report a little further, we would find in graphic terms what the ramifications are going to be in terms of job losses in the next few months.
I do not need to take you through that, Mr. Speaker, because every fisherman, every plant worker, is aware of the dire possibilities for their industry and for their livelihood. That is why I raised the question in June and since then, and that is why I gave notice in June that I was not satisfied. I am still not satisfied with the answers I am getting from the government.
I want to know, and I hope the parliamentary secretary will tell us, why they have their blinkers on in terms of this issue. More to the point, what will they do to help mitigate the issue, to offset the serious dimensions of this problem being faced by fishermen and plant workers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-IMPACT OF FREE TRADE AGREEMENT ON ATLANTIC CANADA-CRISIS IN ATLANTIC INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic fishery is an essential and fundamental component of the Atlantic and the Canadian economies.
In the period since 1977 the value of output grew by 57 per cent in constant dollars while over-all growth in Atlantic Canada was 42 per cent during the same period. The Atlantic fishing industry is a world class competitor. This government believes that such fundamental strengths combined with the opportunities provided by
the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement guarantee benefits for the Atlantic fishery.
While the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement bodes well for the future of all regions in Canada, the Atlantic region in particular can expect significant economic benefits. Most studies identify Atlantic Canada as a primary beneficiary of the agreement.
The Atlantic fishery in the long term is a winner from the free trade agreement. As tariffs are removed, Canadian processors will have the opportunity to expand production of consumer ready products in Canada. Such diversification will lead to more jobs and an improved economic base for many communities in this country.
This provides a positive note for the important Atlantic fishery. Of course, there are factors which are currently having a negative impact on the fishery. Recent downturns in the resource availability of some stocks are known to us all. Factors such as these have always been a part of the fishing industry. It remains fundamentally sound.
The government has in place a wide range of programs to address short run adjustment problems. These include the Canadian Jobs Strategy, industrial assistance and unemployment insurance which are available to cushion the impact of changes in economic activity on individuals and communities. After a full assessment of the problems in the existing programs, the government will, if necessary, initiate further programs or adjust existing programs to assist the industiy as it has done in the past.
The important issues related to stock assessment and overfishing are being dealt with separately. The Prime Minister has appointed a special committee of cabinet to coordinate the government's response to problems in the northern cod fishery and to look at other Atlantic fisheries issues as appropriate. This committee is chaired by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
With respect to overfishing, among many other things the government has initiated a series of diplomatic initiatives to ensure that the European Community and its member countries realize the effect overfishing is having not only on this vital resource but also on the relationship between Canada and Europe.
This government is fully confident in the measures that it has in place or will put in place to deal with adjustment in the Atlantic fishery. Moreover, there are significant benefits offered by the Canada-U.S. Free

Trade Agreement, and we are in a position to seize on them.

Mr. Speaker, on June 6, 1989,1 asked the Minister of Transport and through the Minister of Transport to the House and through the House to the people of Canada and more particularly to the people who work for VIA Rail in Canada what were the plans that they could rely on for their future as employees and workers of VIA Rail.
The question was based on information on that day or the day previous that was released in The Globe and Mail that indicated that VIA's corporate plan indicated that all of VIA Rail would be cut by at least 50 per cent; all the employees and the routes would be cut by at least 50 per cent. That was on June 6, almost four months ago.
I also questioned the Minister about whether, in consideration of the leaked report in The Globe and Mail and with respect to the corporate plan, it would not be wise and not be in good taste that he would at least let the people who were working for VIA Rail, the 3,000 people the report claimed were going to be laid off make plans for their future, for alternate employment, other employment, retirement, early retirement; or all those things that we are hearing about now in this House.
Essentially, I was asking that since we knew there was going to be some drastic measures taken on VIA Rail, could we at least give the employees of VIA Rail an opportunity to protect their own future.
Last Wednesday, a day which will be remembered, particularly by our friends in Atlantic Canada, northern Ontario, small communities throughout this province, municipalities across this country, as black Wednesday, Canadians learned the severity of the plan that we talked about in June in this House.
On January 15, 1990, VIA will eliminate 18 of its 38 routes. The number of trains running will drop to 191 from a current level of 405. The VIA network will reduce its present size by well over 50 per cent. The Globe and Mail was in fact correct. Its estimation of 3,000 employees directly affected was correct. Over 10,000 employees in Canada, those employees employed by CN
Adjournment Debate
and CP and in the tourist industry, will be indirectly affected.
The reason for my question in June was simply to allow these faithful people who are directly affected in Canada to prepare themselves for that eventuality. Atlantic Canada was disemboweled by the moves of VIA Rail. My greatest concern since the announcement has been the government's decision to eliminate The Canadian, a line that runs a passenger rail service through northern Ontario. Commencing on January 15 of next year, the 150,000 northern Ontario residents of Sudbury, the 1,000 residents from Chapleau, the 2,500 from White River, 5,000 residents in Marathon, the 2,500 residents in Terrace Bay, the 120,000 residents in Thunder Bay, the 1,000 people who live in Ignace, the 10,000 people who live in Dryden, the 10,000 who live in Kenora, all along that CP line, will be denied access to passenger rail service in our country. A total of over 350,000 residents in northern Ontario will be denied this service.
Instead, this government has chosen to provide VIA service cross-country three times a week by continuing the cross-country rail line through a route what we used to refer to as the continental line, or the old CN line that starts about 30 miles north when it leaves Toronto, goes up north, about 30 miles north of Sudbury from Capreol, travels the northern route through smaller communities and finds its way into Winnipeg. It goes through Sioux Lookout, Nakina and places like that.
As a result of this very vital decision that affects northern Ontario, the government has chosen to go by the northern CN route, which will have a population of about 5,000 people, rather than the route that was formerly occupied by The Canadian on the north shore of Lake Superior which gives the opportunity to 350,000 people from northern Ontario to still avail themselves of passenger rail service in our country.
I know the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport is prepared to answer this query today and I would ask, in closing, since this so affects the people of northern Ontario, could he restrict himself to that answer alone. Why did the government choose to go on a northern route with only 5,000 people who could avail themselves of passenger rail service rather than taking the other route that would allow 350,000 people from northern Ontario to avail themselves of passenger rail service? Thank you for this opportunity, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon for giving us the opportunity of once again explaining to the Canadian people some of the more difficult decisions that have

October 10, 1989
had to be made in the transportation portfolio during these past few days.
As far as reductions in service in northern Ontario are concerned, the hon. member knows that in order to maintain the national service that is affordable and sustainable, we have had to make a very difficult decision. He knows a commitment has been made to service those comunities that have had no other forms of transportation.
All of those considerations had to be taken into account in order to meet the fiscal responsibilities, the realities which are facing us, and that the new system must be affordable.
The larger northern Ontario communities that the member has referred to have transportation alternatives which remain in place and which have the capacity to take up the slack and we expect will continue to serve the population in these areas.
I believe that the minister was quite clear last week when he made the announcement concerning VIA Rail's five year corporate plan. It is the government's intention that a restructured VIA will result in a national rail passenger network that is, as I have said before, affordable and sustainable. One of the most difficult decisions that had to be made in this restructuring process is that it would mean a reduction, as he has already mentioned, of some 38 per cent of the existing workforce. I think around 2,700 is the more correct figure, not 3,000 that he read in the paper a few months back.
The minister announced that VIA's five year plan makes provision for separation benefits for those af-
Adjoumment Debate
fected employees totalling more than $140 million. VIA has one of the best separation packages available. Additionally, our government has specifically directed VIA to treat all affected employees with generosity and in the fullest compliance with all the applicable collective agreements and legal requirements that are already in place. While that is not a job, nonetheless it does help cushion the blow that will befall some of these people.
In closing, I would like to say that the government does have a host of services and programs, through the Department of Employment and Immigration, such as the industrial adjustment services, and the Canadian Jobs Strategy, that will also help workers to find new jobs and to acquire new skills.
This action has had to be taken because VIA was inefficient, ineffective, and in 1988 it cost a subsidy of some $641 million, and that was rising. It represented a subsidy of $1.5 million a day. Canadians will understand, I am sure, when they finally see the enormity of what we were putting out and what it was continuing to grow into when they see how we are trying to shrink that subsidy.
It is with regret that VIA is going to have to be cancelled out of some of the communities that it now services.
